latin: Grātiās tibi! Fūmāriolum<sup>2</sup> jam implēvī<sup>3</sup>. Habēsne ignem<sup>4</sup>?
Nōlīte fūmum facere, inquit domna cum cane parvulō, fūmī mē taedet<sup>5</sup>.
Doleō, optima domna, sed hoc est loculāmentum fumātōrium, ergō nōbīs tabācō fruī<sup>6</sup> licet, respondet domnus, fūmāriolum tranquillē accendēns<sup>7</sup>.
Impudēns es lēnō<sup>8</sup>! Haec verba prōferēns<sup>9</sup> domna fūmāriolūm arripit idque per fenestram prōjicit<sup>10</sup>.
Mālō tacēre quid sīs, optima domna! Haec verba prōferēns domnus canem parvulum arripit<sup>11</sup>, eumque per fenestram prōjicit...
Silentium sepulcrāle sequitur... audītur tandem frēnōrum strepitus. Trāmen in statiōne quādam cōnsistit.
Tunc, rēs mīrābilis, in crepīdine statiōnis appāret canis parvulus anhēlāns<sup>12</sup> atque dentibus<sup>13</sup> tenēns ... quid enim tenēre possit?
Minimē! Errāvistī! Dentibus tenet ... partem glaciēī quae in thermopōliō lēctiōnis trīcēsimae sextae dēerat!
latinAccented: Grā́tiās tibi! Fūmāríolum<sup>2</sup> jam implḗvī<sup>3</sup>. Habḗsne ignem<sup>4</sup>?
Nōlī́te fūmum fácere, inquit domna cum cane párvulō, fūmī mē taedet<sup>5</sup>.
Dóleō, óptima domna, sed hoc est loculāméntum fumātṓrium, ergō nōbīs tabā́cō fruī<sup>6</sup> licet, respóndet domnus, fūmāríolum tranquíllē accéndēns<sup>7</sup>.
Ímpudēns es lēnō<sup>8</sup>! Haec verba prṓferēns<sup>9</sup> domna fūmāríolūm árripit idque per fenéstram prṓjicit<sup>10</sup>.
Mālō tacḗre quid sīs, óptima domna! Haec verba prṓferēns domnus canem párvulum árripit<sup>11</sup>, eúmque per fenéstram prṓjicit...
Siléntium sepulcrā́le séquitur... audī́tur tandem frēnṓrum strépitus. Trāmen in statiṓne quādam cōnsístit.
Tunc, rēs mīrā́bilis, in crepī́dine statiṓnis appā́ret canis párvulus anhḗlāns<sup>12</sup> atque déntibus<sup>13</sup> tenēns ... quid enim tenḗre possit?
Mínimē! Errāvístī! Déntibus tenet ... partem glaciḗī quae in thermopṓliō lēctiṓnis trīcḗsimae sextae dḗerat!
english: Do you want a cigarette, sir?
Thank you! I have already filled [my] pipe. Do you have [a light] (fire)?
Don’t[pl.] [smoke] (want to make smoke), says the lady with the tiny dog, [smoke disturbs me] (of-smoke me it-disgusts).
I’m sorry, [dear] (excellent) lady, but this is a smoking compartment, therefore it is allowed for us to [smoke] (enjoy with-tobacco), responds the gentleman, tranquilly lighting [his] pipe.
You are an impudent panderer! [With] (bringing forth) these words, the lady takes hold of the pipe and throws it out (through) the window.
I prefer [not to say] (to be silent) what you are, dear lady! With these words, the gentleman takes hold of the tiny dog, and throws it out the window…
A sepulchral silence follows… finally the noise of the brakes is heard. The train comes to a stop at a station.
Then, wondrous thing, on the platform of the station appears the tiny dog, panting and holding [in] (with) its teeth … what indeed could it be holding?
Hmmm… the pipe, I would answer! (perfect subj.)
Not at all! You have made a mistake! In its teeth it holds … the block of ice which was missing [from] (in) the canteen of lesson thirty-six(th)!

footnotes: Hispanicus, -a, -um, Spanish, whence hispanica, cigarette (the Spanish one). Tabacum, -i, n., tobacco; tabaceus, -a, -um, of tobacco. In the exercise: volumen, -inis, n., a rolling, whence volumen tabaceum, cigar.
Fumariolum, -i, n., place from which smoke escapes, little furnace.
Ignis, -is, m., fire. Think of igneous, ignite, ignition, etc.

Me taedet, me paenitet are impersonal verbs; literally, it disgusts me of…, it sorrows me of… The real subject (here me) is in the accusative while the object is in the genitive. Example paenitet Johannem culpae suae: John repents of his offense.
Fruor, -eris, -i, fructus sum + abl. = to profit from, to enjoy.
Accendens, present participle of accendo, -is, -ere, accendi, accensum, to set fire to, to light.
Leno, lenonis, m., slave-dealer, pimp, not a very commendable profession, one suspects.
Profero, -fers, -ferre, -tuli, -latum, irregular like fero, bring forth, advance, mention.
Projicio, -is, -ere, -jeci, -jectum = pro + jacio, throw out, throw away. Pro, in front of, or instead of.

Arripio, -is, -ere, arripui, arreptum = ad + rapio, -is, -ere, rapui, raptum, to take hold of. You will note that rapio, to carry off, does not have exactly the same principal parts as arripio. Often derived verbs depart somewhat from the original, generally for reasons of ease of pronunciation.
Dens, dentis, m., tooth; notice that this word is masculine (unlike its French equivalent la dent). Dens serrae, sawtooth (literally or as a geometric shape).
comments: N.B.— The purely accidental coincidence between Bis Bini, (-ae, -a) and the abbreviation BB is due to the fact that B is the 2nd letter of the Roman alphabet.
Unknown words are going to slip more and more often into our exercises. Today they are particularly numerous:

Capsa, box, whose diminutive capsula, little box, you can also note; natalicius, -a, -um, relating to birth; volumen, see N. 1; acta diurna, literally things done (past participle of ago) during the day (daily); and hence the reporting of them, i.e., formerly chronicle and now newspapers. Chartula, -ae, little card. Septemtrio, -onis, m., the north; flare, to blow; quorsus? in what direction? But you have already seen cursualis in Lesson 22, as well as bis, adv., twice and bini, -ae, -a, in twos, in lesson 6.

latin: Quis (tabācea) volūmina cupit? Mihi est capsa vīgintī quīnque volūminum quam āvia nātāliciō diē meō mihi dōnō dedit.
Hispānicās mālō. Tabacum ipse in papȳrō involvō.
Possumne tabacum in statiōnis thermopōliō emere?
Ita, domne, sed adest quoque taberna in crepīdine, ubi vēndunt tabacum, ācta diurna, chartulāsque cursuālēs.
Hae chartulae mihi placent: duās emam.
Tertiaque emenda est. Certum facere dēbēmus Jacobum amīcum dē adventū nostrō.
Problēma. — Locomotrix typī quī BB dīcitur, quia bis bīnōs axēs habet, orientem petit. Ventus ā septemtriōne flat. Quōrsum it fūmus?
Respōnsum. — Nūllus est fūmus quia locomotrīcēs BB electricae sunt.
latinAccented: Quis (tabā́cea) volū́mina cupit? Mihi est capsa vīgíntī quīnque volū́minum quam ā́via nātālíciō diē meō mihi dōnō dedit.
Hispā́nicās mālō. Tábacum ipse in papȳ́rō invólvō.
Possúmne tábacum in statiṓnis thermopṓliō émere?
Ita, domne, sed adest quoque tabérna in crepī́dine, ubi vēndunt tábacum, ācta diúrna, chartulā́sque cursuā́lēs.
Hae chártulae mihi placent: duās emam.
Tertiáque eménda est. Certum fácere dēbḗmus Jácobum amī́cum dē advéntū nostrō.
Problḗma. — Locómotrix typī quī BB dī́citur, quia bis bīnōs axēs habet, oriéntem petit. Ventus ā septemtriṓne flat. Quōrsum it fūmus?
Respṓnsum. — Nūllus est fūmus quia locomotrī́cēs BB eléctricae sunt.
english: Who wishes for cigars? I have a box of twenty-five cigars that my grandmother gave me as a gift on my birthday.
I prefer cigarettes. I roll the tobacco in paper myself.
Can I buy tobacco in the station(‘s) canteen?
Yes, sir, but there is also a shop on the platform, where they sell tobacco, newspapers, and postcards.
I like these cards: I’ll buy two.
[I must write] (it is necessary I should write) to [my] mother, and to my brother.
And [I must buy] a third (is to-be-bought). We should [inform] (make more-certain) our friend James about our arrival.
Problem.— A locomotive of the type (which is) called BB, because it has twice two axles, is makinf for the west. The wind blows from the north. In what direction does the smoke go?
Answer.—There is no smoke because BB locomotives are electric.
